A Retrospective Comparative Study of 3-Month Early Outcomes Between L-Unitary Soft Endoscopy-Assisted Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion and Conventional Open Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion for Single-Level Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy
abstract: Abstract Objective To compare the 3-month early clinical outcomes of L-Unitary Soft Endoscopy (LUSE)-assisted anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) versus conventional open ACDF in the treatment of single-level cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM), and to evaluate the perioperative safety and early feasibility of LUSE-assisted ACDF, thereby providing a reference for clinical decision-making. Methods A retrospective comparative study was conducted on patients with single-level CSM who underwent ACDF at our hospital between January 2025 and June 2026. Patients were divided into two groups according to the surgical approach: the LUSE-assisted ACDF group (Group A) and the conventional open ACDF group (Group B). Perioperative parameters (operative time, intraoperative blood loss, incision length, length of hospital stay, and perioperative complications) were recorded. The Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score, JOA improvement rate, and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) scores for overall neck/shoulder pain were assessed preoperatively and at 3 months postoperatively and compared between the two groups. The 1-month postoperative assessment was used primarily for safety monitoring. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 27.0. Results A total of 63 patients were enrolled, including 30 in Group A and 33 in Group B. No statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in baseline characteristics, including age, sex, height, weight, BMI, and affected segment (P > 0.05). Compared with Group B, Group A had a significantly shorter operative time, less intraoperative blood loss, and a shorter incision length (P < 0.05). No statistically significant difference was found in length of hospital stay between the two groups (P > 0.05). At 3 months postoperatively, both groups showed significant improvements in JOA scores, JOA improvement rates, and VAS scores for overall neck/shoulder pain compared with preoperative values (P < 0.05), with no statistically significant between-group differences in any of these outcomes (P > 0.05).No severe complications occurred in either group during the 1-month safety monitoring period, and the difference in complication rates was not statistically significant (P > 0.05). Conclusion Compared with conventional open ACDF, LUSE-assisted ACDF for single-level CSM showed no statistically significant difference in early neurological improvement at 3 months, while offering advantages including a smaller incision, less intraoperative blood loss, and a shorter operative time. These findings indicate that LUSE-assisted ACDF is technically feasible and safe in this preliminary series.

title: Patient, relative, visitor, and public perspectives on violence against healthcare workers: a scoping review of reported reasons and prevention approaches
abstract: Abstract Background Workplace violence (WPV) in healthcare threatens healthcare workers’ safety and well-being and may undermine patient care. Patients, relatives, and visitors account for a substantial proportion of reported incidents, particularly in emergency departments. Yet most research has focused on healthcare workers, and less is known about how healthcare users and members of the public explain violence and its circumstances. This review mapped reported reasons, attitudes, intentions, perceived triggers, contextual conditions, and proposed prevention approaches. Methods This scoping review followed Arksey and O’Malley, Levac et al., and JBI guidance and was reported in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and DergiPark were searched on October 24, 2024 (publications through September 30, 2024), and again on October 22, 2026 (publications from October 1, 2024, through October 22, 2026). Eligibility of peer-reviewed empirical studies was defined using the Population–Concept–Context framework. Studies reporting only healthcare workers’ perspectives or predicting violence risk from clinical or administrative data were excluded. Data were independently charted and synthesized descriptively. Quantitative studies were appraised using the JBI analytical cross-sectional checklist, and qualitative studies and components using the CASP qualitative checklist. Results Fourteen studies were included, ten from Türkiye and one each from Palestine, Egypt, Israel, and China. Five studies reported previous violent behavior disclosed by participant subgroups, with estimates ranging from approximately 7% to 20%, depending on the form assessed. Frequently reported reasons and contextual conditions included long waits and treatment delays, overcrowding, inadequate staffing, insufficient information, perceived disregard, and unmet expectations. Proposed prevention approaches addressed communication and interpersonal practice, service organization, public education and media engagement, and legal deterrence or security. No study prospectively evaluated a prevention intervention. Conclusion Healthcare users and members of the public most often explained violence toward healthcare workers in relation to organizational and interactional conditions, particularly waiting, crowding, information gaps, perceived disregard, and unmet expectations. These findings identify priorities for service improvement and future evaluation, but do not establish the effectiveness of any prevention strategy. The small, geographically concentrated, and predominantly cross-sectional evidence base limits causal interpretation and transferability.

Ethical tensions surrounding resistance to care in older adults with neurocognitive disorders: a qualitative study of emergency department professionals’ experiences
abstract: Abstract Purpose Resistance to care (RTC) in older adults with neurocognitive disorders can be difficult to distinguish from refusal of care and may create ethical uncertainty in the emergency department (ED). The aim is to explore ED healthcare professionals’ experiences of RTC among older adults with neurocognitive disorders. Methods We conducted a multicentre qualitative study inspired by grounded-theory methodology. Semi-structured individual interviews were conducted with physicians, junior doctors, registered nurses and advanced practice nurses working in three hospitals in the Île-de-France region. Interviews were analysed through experiential coding, category development, thematic analysis and integrative modelling. Results Twelve professionals were interviewed between 5 March and 17 April 2024. Five themes were identified: the variable and fluctuating nature of RTC; ED-specific contextual factors; staff experiences; ethical questions and ways of addressing them; and care strategies adapted to RTC. Participants described tension between providing necessary care and recognising possible expressions of the person’s wishes. Relational care, family involvement, team discussion and reassessment of the benefit–risk balance supported individualised decisions. Conclusion RTC placed ED staff in situations where clinical urgency, decision-making capacity and respect for the person’s wishes could conflict. Decision support should combine assessment of potentially reversible causes, capacity-sensitive communication and collegial adaptation of the care plan.

Preface 02 · The five-branch coupling Position F071 establishes chemical interpretation; F072 defines contact; F073 qualifies thermal context; F074 integrates qualified observations; F075 audits calibration through time. Evidence Every handoff carries units, time, independent uncertainty and a validity mask. Boundary No common residual or model confidence can authorize actuation on a person. Preface 03 · Observe before intervening Position Classical Chinese acupuncture values careful observation and proportion. The philosophical idea of knowing when to stop motivates independent refusal. Evidence Use chemical activity, force, temperature and clock records as empirical witnesses, never as direct measures of qi or meridians. Boundary Cultural concepts guide questions; they do not substitute for experimental evidence or therapeutic claims. Preface 04 · Chemical observation Position A selective interface responds to activity, transport and matrix conditions, not simply the target label. Evidence The independent assay and reference electrode must support a conditional transfer function with native units. Boundary Matrix-only and reference-only controls may defeat the proposed mechanism. Preface 05 · Contact geometry Position A force sensor does not automatically resolve pressure, and the physical package alters load transfer. Evidence Record independently measured load, real contact area, orientation, and history. Boundary When geometry is unobserved, the local pressure field remains unresolved. Preface 06 · Thermal context Position Temperature influences chemical equilibrium and mechanical expansion; a thermometer has its own thermal dynamics. Evidence A traceable bath, separate timebase and independent readout-power ledger distinguish source changes from probe effects. Boundary A clock correction is not evidence of temperature accuracy. Preface 07 · The fusion paradox Position Averaging independent errors may reduce variance. Shared error persists; identical agreement can conceal a common bias. Evidence Track covariance and systematic uncertainty with independently anchored test cases. Boundary Never infer accuracy from agreement without reference independence. Preface 08 · What self-calibration means Position A calibration map connects an indication to a known physical source. A model that estimates relative drift does not automatically establish an absolute reference. Evidence Challenge offset and gain with separately qualified levels and unseen histories. Boundary Unknown common drift and source changes must remain unresolved when evidence cannot separate them. Preface 09 · The strong conventional rival Position A commercial calibrated conventional sensor is the source-prescribed comparator, not an intentionally weak baseline. Evidence Match source access, timing, allowed calibration and acquisition budget; compare native-unit residual and uncertainty. Boundary If the conventional sensor wins under a fair comparison, the proposed advantage is rejected. Preface 10 · Negative controls as knowledge Position Blank or zero-load cases can expose a falsely positive reading. A constant-source thermal case can reveal drift. Evidence Retain full denominators, interrupted trials and blind reference swaps. Boundary Do not reinterpret failed cases after seeing the desired direction of effect. Preface 11 · The geometry of uncertainty Position The 30 inherited statements include five branch identities and shared statistics; 42 surfaces show analytic slices rather than experimental results. Evidence Each model has axis units, declared assumptions and a deterministic parameter grid. Boundary A surface is not a verified sensor calibration, and a favorable region is not a clinical safety envelope. Preface 12 · Bounded AI inference Position AI can propose a correction or detect a conflict in an offline analysis, but it cannot turn a missing sensor into a measured state. Evidence Include covariance, sample age, calibration validity, model version and a separate refusal record. Boundary A learned prediction may be useful as a hypothesis; it must not receive unearned physical authority. Preface 13 · Nano and quantum boundaries Position Miniaturized sensor interfaces may improve spatial access while increasing sensitivity to surface and packaging effects. Evidence Any proposed quantum measurement advantage must compete against a classical reference with matched data and resources. Boundary This family contains classical analytic models only; no quantum experiment or clinical efficacy is demonstrated. Preface 14 · A future laboratory Position A research gate should survive a new investigator, an inconvenient negative case and a changed instrument. Evidence Archive source standards, unit-tagged raw readings, versioned code, uncertainty, and reasons for refusal. Boundary The source blueprint supplies the roster and formulas. title: Implementation Challenges and Unintended Consequences of Performance-Based Payment: A Qualitative Study of Hospital Managers in Iran
abstract: Abstract Background: Performance-based payment is now widely used to improve efficiency and accountability in healthcare systems. In Iran, this model was introduced under the Health Transformation Plan with the aim of enhancing hospital performance and staff motivation; however, emerging evidence points to notable challenges in its implementation. While previous research has largely examined providers' responses, far less attention has been paid to how hospital managers—those directly responsible for implementing these policies—interpret and manage these incentives in practice. This study explores managers' perspectives on how performance-based payment operates in practice and where they perceive its primary shortcomings. Objective: To explore how public hospital managers interpret, implement, and critically assess performance-based payment, with a particular focus on its operational challenges and unintended consequences. Materials and methods: This qualitative study employed a conventional content analysis approach. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 11 public hospital managers selected through purposive sampling with maximum variation. Data collection continued until thematic saturation was achieved. Analysis followed an iterative process involving open coding, category development, and abstraction of themes. Trustworthiness was ensured using Lincoln and Guba's criteria. Results: Four main themes emerged: imbalance in motivational drivers, threats to organizational commitment, quality–quantity trade-offs, and structural inefficiencies. Although participants acknowledged the system's potential to differentiate performance and support cost control, they consistently highlighted delayed payments—often extending to 6–8 months—alongside limited transparency in calculation mechanisms and perceived inequities in distribution. These challenges were described as weakening the intended motivational effects of the system and were, in some cases, associated with reduced organizational attachment, increased emphasis on service volume over quality, and tendencies toward dual practice. Conclusion: The effectiveness of performance-based payment in public hospitals appears to be shaped less by its formal design than by the conditions under which it is implemented. Delayed payments, constrained managerial discretion, and limited transparency emerged as key factors undermining its intended impact. Addressing these requires more timely and transparent payment processes alongside greater organizational flexibility— findings that carry implications for other health systems confronting analogous reform challenges.

title: Sustainability of a nonpharmacological, self-managed intervention for chronic musculoskeletal pain: a three-group randomized controlled pilot trial
abstract: Abstract Background Chronic musculoskeletal pain (CMP) affects around 1.7 billion people globally, causing significant physical, psychological, and economic burdens. Current treatments often involve medications with risks, creating an urgent need for accessible alternatives. Interventionist-administered auricular point acupressure (APA) has been studied as a nonpharmacologic approach for pain management. This study explored the digital expansion of this low-risk, non-invasive, non-pharmacologic, and non-opioid pain relief method. We developed a self-managed program using mobile health technology (mHealth) and a mobile application for APA (mAPA). The program incorporated coaching videos and real-time feedback collection, enabling individuals to self-administer APA and allowing evaluation of its impact and sustainability. Methods A 3-group pilot randomized controlled trial was conducted among 37 participants with CMP. The participants were randomly assigned to in-person APA ( n = 14) with face-to-face APA instruction, self-guided APA ( n = 12) with remote APA coaching, or control ( n = 11). All participants received conventional healthcare. The APA groups also received a 4-week adjunctive APA intervention supplemented with mobile application coaching videos and were followed monthly for 3 months. Data on pain intensity, physical disability, physical function, anxiety, depression, fatigue, sleep disturbance, fear avoidance of work, and satisfaction were collected at baseline, immediately following the 4-week APA intervention, and during the 2-month and 3-month follow-ups post-intervention. Results Across follow-up assessments, the in-person and self-guided APA groups showed average reductions in pain intensity of approximately 47% from baseline. At least 50% of participants in each APA group achieved at least a 30% reduction in pain intensity across assessment points, and 17% to 36% achieved a 30% reduction in physical disability. The APA groups showed an average increase of 18% in physical function, as well as changes in fatigue, sleep disturbance, and depression. At the 3-month follow-up, fear-avoidance of work had decreased by 50% and 79% from baseline in the in-person and self-guided APA groups, respectively. In contrast, the initial waitlist control group showed increases from baseline in several outcomes at the immediate post-intervention assessment. At the 3-month follow-up, 3.8% of participants reported dissatisfaction with APA. No participant-reported adverse events related to APA were reported during the study period. Conclusion In this pilot trial, the APA groups showed descriptive reductions from baseline in pain intensity and fear avoidance of work, as well as changes in physical disability, physical function, and selected psychological outcomes, through the 3-month follow-up. Mobile application–supported coaching may provide a feasible approach for supporting self-administration of APA and may extend access by enabling remote instruction and guidance. Larger, adequately powered trials are needed to evaluate clinical outcomes, long-term sustainability, potential mechanisms, and the role of APA as an adjunct within multidisciplinary pain-management strategies. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT05020470; First submitted: 08/19/2021.

title: Rapid Wastewater and Environmental Surveillance Informed Precautionary Public Health Action Following the 2024 Kiteezi Landfill Disaster in Uganda
abstract: Abstract Background Wastewater and environmental surveillance (WES) has been used to detect pathogen signals during pandemics and mass gatherings, yet its role in sudden-onset environmental disasters remains poorly understood. Following the catastrophic August 9, 2024, Kiteezi landfill collapse in Kampala, Uganda, which caused fatalities, displaced communities, destroyed sanitation infrastructure, and contaminated the surrounding environment with leachate and sewage, the Ministry of Health rapidly deployed WES to assess infectious disease risks and guide emergency public health action. Methods Between 10 and 12 August 2024, with sampling initiated within 72 hours of the collapse, we conducted a purposive cross-sectional assessment at five high-risk sites: a leachate-floodwater interface, a flowing leachate stream, two stagnant wastewater pools, and a community borehole. Moore swabs were collected at Sites A-D, and a 500 mL grab sample was collected at Site E. Concentrated extracts were qualitatively tested using commercial qPCR or RT-qPCR assays for selected enteric, respiratory, and zoonotic pathogens. The borehole sample was also cultured for Escherichia coli as an indicator of fecal contamination, and field observations documented potential exposure pathways. Results Nucleic acids from Shigella spp., Salmonella spp., non-O1/non-O139 Vibrio cholerae, enteric adenovirus 40/41, selected enteroviruses, SARS-CoV-2, and rotaviruses A-C were detected in one or more leachate or wastewater samples. We did not detect influenza A and B viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, or mpox virus. In the single borehole sample, Escherichia coli and all molecular targets were not detected; this single grab-sample result does not establish that the water source was safe. Field observations identified potential exposure pathways, including unprotected contact with contaminated water, children's proximity to polluted pools, livestock access to leachate, and inadequate protection of a community borehole. The response team reported implementing precautionary measures, including water-source restrictions, household water treatment, access controls, WASH activities, animal-control measures, and enhanced clinical surveillance. These measures were implemented within the broader disaster response, with environmental surveillance findings informing risk assessment and decision-making alongside field observations and other operational information. Conclusions Rapid deployment of WES after the Kiteezi landfill disaster was operationally feasible and produced site-specific evidence of environmental microbial hazards. When combined with field observations and routine disaster-response information, these findings informed precautionary public health decision-making, including drinking-water protection and exposure-reduction measures. Although the assessment did not establish the effectiveness of these interventions in preventing infections, it demonstrated the potential value of integrating environmental surveillance into early disaster-response frameworks. Future applications should incorporate repeated environmental sampling, linked clinical surveillance, and systematic documentation of public health actions and outcomes.

title: Legal Protection of Students’ Rights to Education and Health Amid Forest and Land Fire Haze in Palangka Raya City
journal: Sujud: Jurnal Agama, Sosial dan Budaya
abstract: Forest and land fires that cause haze in Palangka Raya City affect the fulfillment of students’ rights to education and health. This study aims to analyze the legal protection of these two rights and the responsibilities of local governments and educational institutions in addressing emergency haze conditions. This study employs a normative legal research method with statutory and conceptual approaches through an examination of regulations relating to the rights to education and health, child protection, and disaster management. The results of the discussion indicate that legal protection can be provided through adjustments to learning methods, the implementation of distance learning, air quality monitoring, restrictions on outdoor activities, and the provision of health services. However, implementation continues to face obstacles, including limited digital devices, restricted internet access, inter-agency coordination challenges, and unequal access to services. Therefore, stronger coordination, the provision of alternative learning methods, policy evaluation, and sustainable forest and land fire prevention are necessary to ensure the balanced fulfillment of students’ rights to education and health.

title: Patterns of HIV Care and Livelihood Experiences among People Living with HIV following Flood Events in Rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
abstract: Abstract Background KwaZulu-Natal (KZN) has experienced recurrent floods, with the April 2022 floods regarded as among the most devastating in South Africa’s recorded history. We examined how flood-related extreme weather events shaped healthcare utilisation, HIV treatment continuity and livelihood experiences among people living with HIV (PLHIV) in rural KwaZulu-Natal. Methods We conducted an exploratory qualitative descriptive study in Hlabisa, uMkhanyakude District, KwaZulu-Natal. We conducted individual in-depth interviews with 26 PLHIV and four key informants. Six of the interviewed PLHIV also took part in a focus group discussion, and eight community health workers took part in a second focus group discussion. We analysed the data thematically using NVivo 15. Results Participants described how flooding disrupted healthcare access, livelihoods and well-being. Damaged roads, flooded rivers, and transport disruptions hindered access to HIV services, while livelihood losses contributed to food insecurity and emotional distress. Adaptive HIV service strategies, such as multi-month antiretroviral therapy dispensing and community-based delivery, provided some protection against prolonged treatment interruption, although their effectiveness depended on accessible routes, functioning facilities and available outreach capacity. Conclusions Our findings suggest that maintaining HIV services alone may not address the wider consequences of flooding. Climate-resilient HIV programming, including flexible treatment delivery, should be embedded within multisectoral measures that support livelihoods, equitable disaster assistance and community recovery for everyone in flood-affected areas.
